outline.chapter_title: 1. Introduction: Why Mathematical Reasoning Is Hard for LLMs
outline.description: Motivate the study of mathematical reasoning in language models. Describe the gap between closed-source state-of-the-art models and public models, and introduce DeepSeekMath as a research program that pushes the limits of math reasoning in an open setting. Summarize the main contributions and the high-level approach of the paper.
sections: Mathematical reasoning as a distinct capability
Typical failure modes of LLMs on math
Historical progress: from few-shot CoT to tool use and RL
Open vs closed models: performance and accessibility trade-offs
High-level goals of DeepSeekMath
Summary of key contributions (corpus, GRPO, empirical findings)

outline.description: Introduce technical building blocks and prior methods that the book builds on. Provide students with the necessary background: chain-of-thought, program-of-thought, formal theorem proving basics, reinforcement learning for LLMs, and common evaluation paradigms.
sections: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning: concept and examples
Program-of-Thought (PoT) and program-aided reasoning
Tool-integrated reasoning and code-interpreters
Formal mathematics and automated theorem provers (Isabelle, Sledgehammer)
Foundations of reinforcement learning relevant to LLM fine-tuning
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO): objective, advantage, critic
Preference and reward modeling: pairwise comparisons and scalarization
Evaluation metrics: accuracy, self-consistency, Pass@K, Maj@K

outline.chapter_title: 3. Benchmarks and Evaluation Suite for Mathematical Reasoning
outline.description: Detail the datasets and benchmarks used to measure mathematical reasoning. Explain their design, difficulty spectrum, and what each benchmark stresses (quantitative reasoning, competition-level problems, multilingual math, formalization). Describe evaluation protocols, baseline comparisons, and statistical considerations.
sections: GSM8K: grade-school arithmetic reasoning
MATH: competition-level mathematics — scope and challenges
SAT, OCW courses, and other quantitative reasoning datasets
Chinese benchmarks: CMATH, MGSM-zh, Gaokao MathQA and Cloze
miniF2F and informal-to-formal benchmarks
General reasoning and knowledge benchmarks: MMLU, BBH
Code benchmarks: HumanEval and MBPP
Evaluation protocols: few-shot, zero-shot, CoT/PoT prompting, tool-use evaluation
Metrics explained: exact-match, numeric tolerance, self-consistency sampling

outline.chapter_title: 4. Mining Mathematical Data from the Web: Design and Practice
outline.description: Present the process for constructing a large-scale mathematical corpus from Common Crawl. Cover practical steps: deduplication, seed corpora, fastText classifier design, iterative mining, manual URL annotation, and benchmark decontamination. Provide reasoning about each design choice and pitfalls to avoid.
sections: Why use web data? opportunities and risks
Data hygiene: URL-based deduplication and near-deduplication
Choosing seeds: OpenWebMath and other high-quality sources
Training a fastText classifier: model choices and hyperparameters
Iterative mining pipeline: recall, ranking, and expanding the seed set
Domain-level heuristics and manual annotation to increase diversity
Filtering thresholds and how to choose token volume cutoffs
Benchmark contamination: exact-match filtering and strategies
Multilingual handling and coverage considerations
Practical implementation notes and computational costs

outline.chapter_title: 5. Constructing and Validating the DeepSeekMath Corpus
outline.description: Describe the final DeepSeekMath Corpus: size, composition, multilinguality. Explain validation experiments used to establish quality, including pre-training small models and comparing learning curves across corpora (OpenWebMath, MathPile, Proof-Pile-2). Discuss diagnostics used to assess corpus quality.
sections: Overview of the DeepSeekMath Corpus (volume, languages, tokens)
Composition breakdown: web pages, arXiv, AlgebraicStack, code, natural language
Comparison corpora: MathPile, OpenWebMath, Proof-Pile-2
Experimental methodology for corpus validation
Learning curves and epoch effects: why dataset size matters
Evidence for quality: downstream benchmark improvements
Multilingual benefits: English vs Chinese results
Limitations of corpus validation and open questions

outline.description: Explain model initialization and the pre-training strategy used for DeepSeekMath-Base 7B. Cover rationale for starting from a code-trained base, the mixed data distribution, hyperparameter choices, optimizer, and training schedule. Introduce practical considerations for large-scale continual training.
sections: Why start from a code-trained model (DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5)?
Pre-training data mix: math corpus, AlgebraicStack, arXiv, GitHub code, CC text
Compute and training budgets: tokens, context length, batching
Optimization: AdamW parameters, learning rate schedule, warmup
Regularization and stability techniques (weight decay, clip rules)
Checkpointing, reproducibility and logging
Measuring pre-training progress: validation sets and early stopping
Potential failure modes and how to monitor them

outline.description: Present empirical studies exploring how pre-training choices affect performance. Focus on the paper's key ablations: the effect of code training, the role (or lack) of arXiv, and token mixing strategies. Provide analysis and interpretations of results.
sections: Two-stage vs one-stage training setups: experimental design
Effect of code pre-training on program-aided reasoning
Effect of code pre-training on CoT reasoning (no tools)
Mixing strategies: simultaneous code+math vs sequential stages
ArXiv-only experiments: results and hypotheses
Language coverage and multilingual impacts
Discussion: capacity limits and data curriculum
Takeaways for practitioners

outline.chapter_title: 8. Supervised Fine-Tuning and Instruction Tuning for Math
outline.description: Describe the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage: building instruction datasets, annotation formats (CoT, PoT, tool-integrated), multilingual curation, training protocol, and evaluation. Explain design decisions that lead to DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B.
sections: Goals of instruction tuning for mathematical competence
Curating SFT data: sources, annotation procedures, and scale
Annotation formats: CoT, PoT, and tool-integrated reasoning
Chinese and English SFT data: balancing multilingual needs
Training SFT models: context concatenation, batch sizes, learning rates
Evaluation of SFT: benchmarks and baselines
Comparisons to other instruction-finetuned math models
Failure modes and quality control in SFT datasets

outline.chapter_title: 9. Reinforcement Learning for Language Models: Review and Limitations
outline.description: Provide a deep review of RL techniques that have been applied to LLM fine-tuning, focusing on PPO. Explain the actor-critic framework, advantage estimation, the need for KL penalties, computational costs of the value model, and typical reward model design. Discuss why standard PPO can be impractical at scale and motivate the need for alternatives.
sections: Reinforcement learning in LLM fine-tuning: motivations and goals
Actor-critic algorithms and the role of the critic
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in detail
Advantage estimation: GAE and its assumptions
Reward models: training from preferences and comparisons
KL penalty and reference model regularization
Memory and compute burden: the critic and training instability
Practical issues: sparse rewards, noisy labels, and over-optimization

outline.description: Introduce GRPO in depth. Present derivation from PPO, the intuition behind using group-relative baselines, algorithmic details, objective function, outcome vs process supervision, iterative training, and practical hyperparameters. Explain advantages in memory and alignment with preference-model training.
sections: Motivation: why group-based baselines?
Deriving GRPO from PPO: objective comparison
Group sampling: sampling G outputs per question
Group-relative advantage estimation: normalization and formulas
Outcome supervision: single final reward per output
Process supervision: step-wise rewards and cumulative advantages
KL regularization as a loss term vs per-token reward penalty
Iterative GRPO: updating reward models and replay buffers
Algorithm pseudocode and implementation notes
Hyperparameters (G, KL coefficient, learning rates) and tuning tips
Memory and compute benefits vs PPO

outline.chapter_title: 11. Unified Paradigm: Relating SFT, RFT, DPO, PPO and GRPO
outline.description: Present a unified mathematical framework that expresses the gradient updates of different training approaches (SFT, RFT, DPO, online/offline RFT, PPO, GRPO) in a common form. Use this to explain their similarities and differences, and analyze experimental comparisons that illuminate the roles of data source, reward function, and algorithm.
sections: General gradient formulation for sequence training
Components of the paradigm: data source, reward function, algorithm
Mapping SFT, RFT, DPO, online RFT, PPO and GRPO into the framework
Comparative analysis: offline vs online sampling
How algorithms transform reward signals into gradient coefficients
Experimental comparisons and what they reveal (online RFT vs RFT)
Why GRPO's graded coefficient helps relative to RFT
Practical consequences for method selection

outline.description: Describe the end-to-end RL training of DeepSeekMath-RL 7B using GRPO, including reward model construction, training data, sampling choices, iterative updates, and evaluation. Present the key empirical results across benchmarks and analyze improvements and remaining gaps.
sections: Setup: initializing from DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B
Reward model construction and training protocol
Sampling strategy: G=64 outputs, decoding, and length
Outcome vs process supervision experiments
Iterative training with reward model updates and replay
Evaluation results: GSM8K, MATH, CMATH, Gaokao, miniF2F
Self-consistency sampling and its effects
Out-of-domain performance improvements
Comparative results vs closed-source and open-source baselines
Ablations: sample size, KL coefficient, outcome vs process supervision

outline.chapter_title: 13. Analyses: Why Reinforcement Learning Helps and What It Changes
outline.description: Offer deeper analysis about the mechanisms by which RL (specifically GRPO) improves performance. Discuss Maj@K vs Pass@K findings, distribution sharpening, misalignment phenomena, and what RL does to the top-k mass. Provide cautionary notes and implications for future work.
sections: Maj@K and Pass@K: definitions and diagnostics
Empirical findings: RL increases Maj@K but not Pass@K
Interpretation: distribution concentration vs capability improvement
Misalignment in SFT models and preference alignment strategies
Risks of overfitting to reward model blind spots
Robustness to noisy reward signals and potential remedies
Practical diagnostic checks for RL training progress
Lessons for designing reward models and sampling strategies

outline.chapter_title: 14. Practical Guidance: Implementation, Reproducibility and Engineering Trade-offs
outline.description: Provide concrete, actionable guidance for researchers and engineers who want to reproduce or build on DeepSeekMath. Cover data decontamination scripts, checkpointing, reward model pipelines, efficient inference for exploration, memory optimizations, and compute budgeting.
sections: Reproducibility checklist: data, code, seeds, and checkpoints
Decontamination rules and scripts for benchmark filtering
Efficient inference strategies for large-sample exploration

Reward model training pipeline and replay buffer implementation

Hyperparameter recipes and tuning heuristics
Monitoring training: metrics, visualization, and alerts
Ethical considerations and data governance

outline.description: Synthesize the findings, discuss limitations of the current approach (geometry weaknesses, few-shot performance, scale), and propose research directions. Emphasize open problems: better reward models, robust RL, improved data curation, formal math integration, and scaling laws for math reasoning.
sections: Summary of what DeepSeekMath accomplishes

Open questions about dataset biases and coverage
Improving reward models: uncertainty, generalization and process supervision
Robust RL: weak-to-strong alignment and noise-tolerant algorithms
Better exploration: advanced decoding and search strategies
The role of scale vs data quality: empirical trade-offs
Integrating formal and informal math resources
Concluding thoughts and a roadmap for future research
